books.section: Topic 6.13 Politics in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: William Jennings Bryan, “Cross of Gold” speech, July 9, 1896

stimulus.text: Having behind us the producing masses of this nation and the world, supported by the commercial interests, the laboring interests, and the toilers everywhere, we will answer their demand for a gold standard by saying to them: You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns, you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.
stimulus.source_note: William Jennings Bryan, “Cross of Gold” speech, Democratic National Convention, Chicago, July 9, 1896. Public domain; wording and punctuation follow Bryan, The First Battle (1896).

stem: Bryan calls the gold standard a “cross of gold” and a “crown of thorns.” What does this language suggest about how he saw the money question?

options.text: It was a minor detail of banking law
options.misconception: A crown of thorns and a cross are images of suffering, not of a minor detail.

options.text: It was a question only bankers understood
options.misconception: Bryan speaks for laborers and toilers, not only for bankers.

options.text: It was a technical problem with no moral meaning
options.misconception: Religious images of suffering give the question deep moral meaning.

options.text: It was a moral struggle in which labor suffered

rationales.A: Images of a crown of thorns and a cross mark a great suffering, not a detail.
rationales.B: Bryan claims the producing masses understand it, not bankers alone.
rationales.C: The religious images make the question moral, not merely technical.
rationales.D: The crown presses on the brow of labor, so labor is the sufferer.
rationales.general:
Ask what the images do.
1. A crown of thorns and a cross are images of pain and sacrifice.
2. Bryan puts the crown on the brow of labor and mankind on the cross.
3. That makes the gold standard a cause of suffering, not a banking detail.
4. Background from the books: falling prices made debts heavier, so debtors saw gold as a burden.
Remember: religious images in a speech mark a moral fight, not a technical one.
